description: We are five students who built VOIDBOUND, an Arabic browser game that teaches how a real mission to Pluto is designed, with a tight budget, linked systems and hidden consequences. We like turning hard space engineering into something people can play. We are looking for teammates who can help with English translation, voice-over, graphic design or web development to take it further. If you love space and learning by doing, join us.
summary:
VOIDBOUND is a browser game that teaches how a real space mission is designed, using a trip to Pluto as the setting. The player is a grandson finishing his grandfather's dream, with a budget of $110,000 to spend across 18 decisions: crew, ship, life support, and propulsion and landing. Each choice shows only its price. How it affects the mission stays hidden until the end, so players have to reason it out.
Along the way, five emergencies appear: a solar storm, an oxygen alarm, an overheating engine, the asteroid belt, and a crew conflict. The systems also affect each other. An ion engine without a reactor fails, for example, because solar panels get weak far from the Sun. At the end, the game explains every effect through expert notes and a mission report. Leftover money becomes fuel, which is how the rocket equation shows up in play.
It runs on any phone or computer with no install, in Egyptian Arabic, and up to four players can share one device, each with a different role.
details: What it does The player works through four stages (crew, ship, vital systems, propulsion and landing). Each stage has two-option decisions, and every option costs money. After the decisions, five emergencies test the design. The game ends with one of five outcomes (failure, Moon, Mars, Saturn, Pluto) based on a mission success score that stays hidden until the final screen. What it teaches Mission design is a chain of trade-offs between cost, safety, and performance. The rocket equation: fuel grows exponentially with the change in velocity. Ion vs. chemical propulsion: high efficiency, but it needs strong power and time. Nuclear vs. solar power: solar output falls with 1/distance², so it struggles near Pluto. Safety margins: 20% margin on spacecraft systems, power at 120% of demand. Radiation shielding, food systems, deep-space communication, and navigation. Scientific instruments add value but also add mass, power draw, data volume, and cost. The data needs a link strong enough to send it home. Integrated design Hidden interactions are calculated between decisions, for example advanced spectrometer + basic radio = too much data to transmit. They are revealed at the end in "Expert Notes." Team play 2 to 4 players share one device. Roles: Trajectory & Propulsion, Spacecraft & Power, Science & Communications, Crew & Supplies. The final report shows each player's spending and accuracy. Mission Report and sharing Five colored indicators (power, mass, communication, duration, science value). Each game ends with a share code so friends can compare designs. Note: the indicator values are simplified educational units made by our team, not official NASA figures. Tech A single HTML file (~14 MB), plain JavaScript, Web Audio API for sound effects, with embedded videos and images. No libraries, no installation. Impact Space engineering is usually taught in a dry way and mostly in English. VOIDBOUND gives Arabic-speaking students a way to learn it by playing. Next steps Difficulty levels, online multiplayer, an English version, voice-over, a leaderboard.
